messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The intersection on Route 9 had been clear until the delivery truck blew through the red light. Samir remembered the sickening crack of his sedan’s rear bumper, the violent spin across two lanes, and the deafening screech of twisting metal as he was pinned against the steering wheel. When firefighters finally cut him free, the air was thick with the sharp tang of spilled liquor from a nearby cab, and the wail of sirens echoed over the grinding of his own shattered engine. For weeks afterward, the memory did not fade; it returned in sudden, unbidden flashes. A glance at a parked sedan would instantly drag him back to the moment his own car folded like paper, while the faint whiff of bourbon from a passing driver’s cup would tighten his chest until he was certain another crash was inevitable. As the months passed, these intrusions quickly escalated into a permanent state of physical alarm. Every time the crash imagery surfaced or he caught the smell of alcohol in the air, his heart would hammer against his ribs and his shoulders would hike up instinctively. He was never truly at ease, his nervous system locked in a constant scan for danger. This heightened threat state meant that ordinary office doors slamming or distant car backfires made him jump as if struck, keeping his hypervigilance dialed to an exhausting maximum. What frightened him most was not the noise or the sights, but the realization that he felt fundamentally broken. He could not rely on himself to navigate a simple commute without his hands shaking, and he was certain he was no longer capable of doing the meticulous work that had defined his career as a tax inspector. Believing he would never again feel normal emotions, Samir began to withdraw. When the crash imagery grew too heavy, he would instinctively retreat to his phone, scrolling through games and endless feeds for hours to drown out the internal noise. He avoided eating because the act of sitting still felt unbearable, and he gave up driving entirely, taking a long detour on the bus just to avoid being anywhere near a steering wheel. This withdrawal only deepened his dread. The longer he sat isolated behind a screen and starved himself, the more he interpreted this paralysis as proof that he was permanently incapable and could no longer rely on himself. Convinced his emotions were permanently gone, he viewed the world through a lens of inherent danger, which in turn amplified his sense of threat every time a loud noise echoed through the hallway. Locked in this perpetual state of alarm, he found his attention irresistibly drawn to the very things he feared, his hyper-alert eyes locking onto matching car models and his nose catching alcohol on passersby, feeding the very intrusions he was trying to escape. His physical exhaustion and mental fatigue from screen addiction left his nerves raw, so ordinary sounds in the downtown tax office now felt like immediate threats. At his desk, the consequences were undeniable. A colleague’s dropped file made him startle violently, and the faint whiff of vanilla liqueur from the breakroom coffee pot sent him scrambling to the stairwell to catch his breath. His audits grew sloppy, missed deadlines piled up, and his supervisor began questioning his reliability after he failed to attend three consecutive client meetings because the thought of leaving his apartment paralyzed him. Divorced for two years and already isolated by the trauma, Samir found himself utterly alone with his unraveling routine. What finally brought him to the clinic was a panic attack during a routine audit review, triggered by the smell of a client’s mint liqueur and the distant thud of a falling folder. He sat on the floor of the supply closet, trembling, terrified that he had permanently lost the ability to function or feel joy again, and desperate for someone to show him how to stop waiting for the next crash.
